notes.urn:cts:latinLit:stoa0171.stoa009.opp-la: The name ‘Fenta’ is unusual and could not be identified; the reading may be corrupt.
Line 3 is corrupt as printed: ‘ei bono … enectum’ is read as ‘ex bono … effectum’ (made out of good), and ‘διβολον’ as διάβολον.

Line 6 begins mid-sentence; ‘whose’ refers to God at the end of line 5. In line 2, ‘(uina)’ appears to be an editorial supplement, translated as [wine], and ‘mroga.ut’ is read as ‘irrogant’ (inflict).

nodes.text: the seventh, the Cumaean, named Amalthea, who is called Herophile or Demophile by others; and that she brought nine books to King Tarquinius Priscus and asked three hundred *philippei* [gold coins] for them, and that the king, scorning the size of the price, laughed at the woman's madness; that she burned three in the king's sight and demanded the same price for the rest; that Tarquin thought the woman much madder still;

How can this be proved? The ancient histories, of course, teach it. Euhemerus, an ancient author who came from the city of Messene, collected the deeds of Jupiter and of the others who are thought to be gods, and wove together a history from the titles and sacred inscriptions that were kept in the most ancient temples, and above all in the shrine of Jupiter Triphylius, where an inscription showed that a golden column had been set up by Jupiter himself, on which column he wrote out his own deeds, so that there might be a record of his achievements for posterity.

So, driven out, he fled and came to Italy by ship, after wandering for a long time, as Ovid reports in the books of the Fasti: ‘The reason for the ship remains: the sickle-bearing god came by ship to the Tuscan river, after first wandering over the world.’ Janus took him in, wandering and destitute:

For when Tarquin wanted to build the Capitol and there were shrines of many gods on that site, he consulted them through auguries as to whether they would yield to Jupiter; and while the rest yielded, Terminus alone stayed. Hence the poet calls him ‘the immovable rock of the Capitol’.

But as Pompilius was the founder of foolish religious rites among the Romans, so before Pompilius was Faunus in Latium, who both established impious rites for his grandfather Saturn and honoured his father Picus among the gods, and consecrated his sister Fenta Fauna, who was also his wife; Gavius Bassus records that she was called Fatua because she used to foretell their fates to women, as Faunus did to men.

For this reason women sacrifice to her in secret and call her the Good Goddess. And Sextus Clodius, in the book he wrote in Greek, reports that she was the wife of Faunus; and that because, against custom and royal propriety, she had secretly drunk off a jar of wine and become drunk, she was beaten to death by her husband with myrtle rods; but that afterwards, when he regretted what he had done and could not bear his longing for her, he conferred divine honour on her; and that for this reason a covered jar of wine is placed at her rites.

But which of them came first in time may be doubted, since Latinus and Priam reigned in the same years, and likewise their fathers Faunus and Laomedon, in whose reign Orpheus came with the Argonauts to the shore of the people of Ilium.

Then he made another, in whom the character of the divine stock did not endure. So he was infected by his own envy as if by poison, and passed over from good to evil, and by his own choice, which had been given to him free by God, he took on himself a contrary name.
From this it is clear that envy is the source of all evils. For he envied that predecessor of his, who by persevering is both approved by God the Father and dear to him.
This one, then, who of himself became evil out of good, the Greeks call *diabolos*; we call him the accuser, because he reports to God the crimes into which he himself entices [men].

So when the number of men had begun to increase, God, taking care lest the devil, to whom he had given power over the earth from the beginning, should by his deceits either corrupt or destroy men, as he had done at the outset, sent angels to guard and to care for the human race; and he commanded them above all not to be stained by the contagion of the earth and so lose the dignity of their heavenly substance. Evidently he forbade them to do what he knew they would do, so that they could not hope for pardon.
And so that most deceitful lord of the earth, through their very familiarity, little by little enticed them into vices as they lived among men, and defiled them by intercourse with women.

Then, not being received into heaven because of the sins in which they had plunged themselves, they fell to the earth. Thus the devil made them, from angels of God, into his own attendants and servants.

But those who were begotten from them, because they were neither angels nor men but bore a kind of intermediate nature, were not received into the underworld, just as their parents were not received into heaven.
So two kinds of demons came into being, one heavenly, the other earthly. These are the unclean spirits, the authors of the evils that are done, and their prince is that same devil.

And so they fill everything with plots, frauds, tricks and errors: for they attach themselves to individual men and occupy all houses, door to door, and take for themselves the name of *genii* [guardian spirits]; for that is how the Latin language renders *daimones*.

[People] consecrate these in their inner shrines, pour out [wine] to these every day, and knowingly venerate demons as if they were earthly gods and as averters of the evils which [the demons] themselves cause and inflict.

Since they are thin spirits that cannot be grasped, they work their way into men's bodies and, operating secretly in their inner organs, they damage health, stir up diseases, terrify souls with dreams and shake minds with frenzies, so as to force men by these evils to run to them for help.

The reasoning behind all these deceptions is obscure to those who have no share in the truth. For they think that those [spirits] help them when they stop harming them, though they can do nothing but harm.

Someone may perhaps say that they should therefore be worshipped, so that they do no harm, since they are able to harm. They do harm, indeed, but to those by whom they are feared, whom the mighty and exalted hand of God does not protect, who are strangers to the sacrament of truth. But the just, that is, the worshippers of God, they fear,

by whose name they are adjured and go out of bodies; and, lashed by their words as if by whips, they not only confess that they are demons but even give out their names, those that are worshipped in the temples. This they generally do in the presence of their own worshippers, to the disgrace, certainly, not of religion but of their own honour, because they can lie neither to God, by whom they are adjured, nor to the just, by whose voice they are tortured.

But magicians, and those whom the common people rightly call *malefici* [evildoers], when they practise their accursed arts, summon them by their true names, those heavenly ones that are read in the holy writings.

If Christ was a magician because he did wonders, then surely Apollonius was more skilled, he who, as you describe, when Domitian wanted to punish him, suddenly vanished from his trial, than the one who was both arrested and fixed to a cross.
